teaser: Carved for a tomb of forty statues that shrank and shrank. He waited thirty years for his place.
review_notes:
Chronology: tomb commissioned 1505; Julius II died February 1513; new contract with heirs May 1513; Moses carved c. 1513-15; further contracts 1516, 1532, 1542; installed 1545. Catalog year 1515 is consistent.
Michelangelo's age in 1513: 38.
Poem about his body bent 'like a bow' from painting the ceiling: sonnet to Giovanni da Pistoia, paraphrased, not quoted.
'Tragedy of the tomb' is the phrase of his biographer Condivi.
Vasari's report that Roman Jews came on Saturdays to admire the statue: check.
Freud's essay 'The Moses of Michelangelo' appeared anonymously in 1914: check.
Knee legend ('Why don't you speak?') is presented as a legend.
Julius II is buried in St. Peter's, not in this monument: check.
Moses was intended for the upper level of the 1513 design: check.
Height 235 cm.
Vasari quote 'like flocks of starlings' (come gli storni): check the wording.
Freud's repeated visits to the statue: check.

lesson.text: In 1513 Michelangelo was 38, famous and worn out. He had just spent four years on a scaffold painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling, head tipped back, paint dripping on his face. In a poem he joked that the job had bent his body like a bow. And he had never wanted to be a painter in the first place.

The man who forced the brush on him, Pope Julius II, died that February. For Michelangelo this was oddly good news. Back in 1505 Julius had ordered his own tomb from him: a marble mountain with some forty statues. Then the pope lost interest and the project stalled for years. Now his heirs signed a fresh contract, and the sculptor could go back to stone.

He rented a house in Rome, had the marble blocks hauled there, and attacked them. The Moses, begun that same year, is 235 cm tall (about 7 ft 8 in) seated. He is the prophet who led his people out of Egypt and came down from Mount Sinai carrying God's law, cut into two tablets of stone.
Those two tablets are in the statue, though Moses seems to have half forgotten them. Where are they?

spots.title: The tablets
spots.text: Two plain slabs stand on edge beside his hip, pinned under his right arm. No writing is visible. They look as if they could slide to the floor at any moment.

lesson.text: Why is he holding the law so carelessly? Because something has caught his attention. In the Bible, Moses returns from the mountain to find his people dancing around a golden idol. Many viewers think this is that moment. He is sitting down, yet nothing in the figure is at rest.

lesson.title: A seated storm
lesson.text: Travel down the figure and count the signs of something about to happen.

spots.title: Horns and a glare
spots.text: The head jerks toward his left, brows knotted. Two short horns rise from the hair. They are no insult: medieval and Renaissance artists gave them to Moses as a sign of holiness.

spots.title: Fingers in the beard
spots.text: The beard pours down like water, in ropes so deeply cut they cast shadows. His right hand has grabbed a handful and drags it sideways, the absent gesture of a man fighting to control himself.

spots.title: The left arm
spots.text: Bare from the shoulder, as thick as a thigh. Veins run over the forearm and the muscles are tight although the hand rests in his lap. Marble has been polished here until it gleams like skin.

spots.title: The leg pulled back
spots.text: His left leg is drawn back into the shadow, the foot set on its toes. It is how you place a leg just before standing up.

lesson.text: The horns come from a translation. The Hebrew Bible says the face of Moses was radiant after he spoke with God. The Latin version read in Western churches turned the word into “horned,” and for centuries artists followed the Latin.

Turned head, clawing hand, coiled leg: is he about to leap up and smash the tablets, as the Bible says he did? Or has he already mastered his fury? People have argued about it for five centuries. Michelangelo's contemporaries had a word for this kind of fearsome energy in his work: terribilità, roughly “awesomeness” that frightens.

Sigmund Freud, the founder of psychoanalysis, was obsessed with this statue and came back to stare at it during his stays in Rome. In 1914 he published an essay arguing that Moses is holding his rage in to save the tablets. He left his name off it.
Michelangelo carved a man sitting still and made stillness look like the hardest thing a body can do.

The good year did not last. In 1516 a new pope from the Medici family pulled Michelangelo away to Florence for other projects. Julius's heirs complained, sued and renegotiated, in 1516, in 1532, in 1542. Each contract meant a smaller tomb. His biographer called the whole affair “the tragedy of the tomb.” Moses sat in the workshop for about thirty years.

When the statue finally went on view, the writer Vasari reported that the Jews of Rome came in groups every Saturday to see it, “like flocks of starlings,” although images of this kind were foreign to their tradition.

The monument was completed in 1545, in the church of San Pietro in Vincoli, not in St. Peter's as Julius had dreamed. Of the forty statues, a handful were made. Moses had been designed for an upper level, to be seen from below. He ended up on the ground floor, in the center, between the carved pillars you see here, far too big for his niche. The pope himself is buried elsewhere.

Rome tells one more story about him. When Michelangelo finished, the statue seemed so alive that he struck its knee with his hammer and shouted, “Why don't you speak?” It is only a legend. Stand in front of that knee, though, and you understand why someone had to invent it.

quiz.question: What had Michelangelo just finished when he began the Moses?
quiz.explanation: He had spent four years painting the ceiling for Julius II.

quiz.question: What was the Moses made for?
options: The tomb of Pope Julius II
quiz.explanation: It was one of some forty statues planned for the pope's tomb.

quiz.question: Why does Moses have horns?
options: To show he was a warrior
The sculptor's chisel slipped and he improvised
A Latin translation of the Bible described his face as horned
quiz.explanation: The Hebrew word for “radiant” was rendered as “horned” in the Latin Bible.

quiz.question: What is his right hand doing?
quiz.explanation: The fingers drag a handful of the long beard to one side.

quiz.question: What did Freud argue about the statue?
options: That Moses is restraining his anger
That it was not by Michelangelo
quiz.explanation: His 1914 essay says Moses masters his rage to save the tablets.

facts.text: The tomb of Julius II was built with the forty statues first planned.
facts.explanation: The project shrank with every contract and only a handful of statues were made.

facts.text: The Moses waited about thirty years before it was installed.
facts.explanation: Carved around 1513 to 1515, it went on view in 1545.

facts.text: The Moses stands in St. Peter's Basilica.
facts.explanation: It is in the church of San Pietro in Vincoli in Rome.
